It then turns to the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin, who were to continue a kingdom after the final captivity of their brethren; and gives first a favorable prognostication of their affairs under Hezekiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.5">Isa 28:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.6">Isa 28:6</reference>; but soon changes to reproofs and threatenings for their intemperance and their profaneness, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.7">Isa 28:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.8">Isa 28:8</reference>. They are introduced as not only scornfully rejecting, but also mocking and ridiculing, the instructions of the prophet, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.9">Isa 28:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.10">Isa 28:10</reference>. To this God immediately retorts in terms alluding to their own mocking, but differently applied, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.11-Isa.28.13">Isa 28:11-13</reference>. The prophet then addresses these scoffers, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.14">Isa 28:14</reference>; who considered themselves as perfectly secure from every evil, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.15">Isa 28:15</reference>; and assures them that there was no method under heaven but one, by which they could be saved, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa 28:16</reference>; that every other vain resource should fail in the day of visitation, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.17">Isa 28:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.18">Isa 28:18</reference>. He then farther adds, that the judgments of God were particularly levelled against them; and that all the means to which they trusted for warding them off should be to no purpose, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.19">Isa 28:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.20">Isa 28:20</reference>; as the Almighty, who, on account of his patience and long-suffering, is amiably described as unacquainted with punishing, had nevertheless determined to punish them, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.21">Isa 28:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.22">Isa 28:22</reference>. The prophet then concludes with a beautiful parable in explanation and defense of God's dealing with his people, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.23-Isa.28.29">Isa 28:23-29</reference>. <div eID="gen27596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27597" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27598" type="x-p"/> Wo to the crown of pride - By the crown of pride, etc., Samaria is primarily understood. "Sebaste, the ancient Samaria, is situated on a long mount of an oval figure, having first a fruitful valley, and then a ring of hills running round about it;" Maundrell, p. 58. "E regione horum ruderum mons est peramoenus, planitie admodum frugifera circumseptus, super quem olim Samaria urbs condita fuit;" Fureri Itinerarium, p. 93. The city, beautifully situated on the top of a round hill, and surrounded immediately with a rich valley and a circle of other hills beyond it, suggested the idea of a chaplet or wreath of flowers worn upon their heads on occasions of festivity, expressed by the proud crown and the fading flower of the drunkards. That this custom of wearing chaplets in their banquets prevailed among the Jews, as well as among the Greeks and Romans, appears from the following passage of the book of The Wisdom of Solomon: - "Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and ointments, <div eID="gen27598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27599" type="x-p"/> And let no flower of the spring pass by us: <div eID="gen27599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27600" type="x-p"/> Let us crown ourselves with rose-buds before they are withered." <div eID="gen27600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27601" type="x-p"/> The Wisdom of Solomon 2:7, 8.
entries.0b5a5d97e292f1c5ccb135d2bbe198dc3985c470: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen27601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27602" type="x-p"/> Behold the Lord hath a mighty and strong one "Behold the mighty one, the exceedingly strong one" - אמץ לאדני ammits ladonai, fortis Domino, i.e., fortissimmus, a Hebraism. For לאדני ladonai, to the Lord, thirty-eight MSS. Of Dr. Kennicott's and many of De Rossi's, with some of my own, and two editions, read ליהוה laihovah, to Jehovah.
entries.27ff04be3f5ad04f6a4945e39d4e0831f3682b48: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27603" type="x-p"/> The crown of pride, the drunkards of Ephraim "The proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim" - I read עטרות ataroth, crowns, plural, to agree with the verb תרמסנה teramasnah, "shall be trodden down."
entries.53cd9fb16f86f5094dd09bce86d14f441545b9ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27604" type="x-p"/> The hasty fruit before the summer "The early fruit before the summer" - "No sooner doth the boccore, (the early fig), draw near to perfection in the middle or latter end of June, than the kermez or summer fig begins to be formed, though it rarely ripens before August; about which time the same tree frequently throws out a third crop, or the winter fig, as we may call it. This is usually of a much longer shape and darker complexion than the kermez, hanging and ripening upon the tree even after the leaves are shed; and, provided the winter proves mild and temperate, is gathered as a delicious morsel in the spring; "Shaw, Travels, p. 370, fol. The image was very obvious to the inhabitants of Judea and the neighboring countries, and is frequently applied by the prophets to express a desirable object; by none more elegantly than by <reference osisRef="Hos.9.10">Hos 9:10</reference> : - "Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel; <div eID="gen27604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27605" type="x-p"/> Like the first ripe fig in her prime, I saw your fathers." <div eID="gen27605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27606" type="x-p"/> Which when he that looketh upon it seeth "Which whoso seeth, he plucketh it immediately" - For יראה yireh, which with הראה haroeh makes a miserable tautology, read, by a transposition of a letter, יארה yoreh; a happy conjecture of Houbigant. The image expresses in the strongest manner the great ease with which the Assyrians shall take the city and the whole kingdom, and the avidity with which they shall seize the rich prey without resistance.
entries.bc8b670ab2065bacce45b3b7d382f47287c218fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27607" type="x-p"/> In that day - Thus far the prophecy relates to the Israelites, and manifestly denounces their approaching destruction by Shalmaneser. Here it turns to the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin, the remnant of God's people who were to continue a kingdom after the final captivity of the Israelites. It begins with a favorable prognostication of their affairs under Hezekiah; but soon changes to reproofs and threatenings for their intemperance, disobedience, and profaneness. <div eID="gen27607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27608" type="x-p"/> Jonathan's Targum on this verse is worthy of notice: "In that time Messiah, the Lord of hosts משיחא דיי צבאות meshicha dayai tsebaoth, shall be a crown of joy and a diadem of praise to the residue of his people." Kimchi says the rabbins in general are of this opinion. Here then the rabbins, and their most celebrated Targum, give the incommunicable name, יהוה צבאות Yehovah tsebaoth, the Lord of hosts, to our ever blessed Redeemer, Jesus Christ.
entries.262f30e7301991dbedce4d663d884fcb9934e90f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27609" type="x-p"/> The battle to the gate "The war to the gate of the enemy" - That is, who pursue the fleeing enemy even to the very gates of their own city. "But we were upon them even unto the entering of the gate," <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.23">2Sam 11:23</reference>; that is, we drove the enemy back to their own gates. See also <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.52">1Sam 17:52</reference>. The Targum says, The Messiah shall give the victory to those who go out to battle, that he may bring them back to their own houses in peace.
entries.fbdbbaa6998d5224e545625eaf0ddefd682019f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen27609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27610" type="x-p"/> Whom shall he teach knowledge?" Whom, say they, would he teach knowledge?" - The scoffers mentioned below, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.14">Isa 28:14</reference>, are here introduced as uttering their sententious speeches; they treat God's method of dealing with them, and warning them by his prophets, with contempt and derision. What, say they, doth he treat us as mere infants just weaned? doth he teach us like little children, perpetually inculcating the same elementary lessons, the mere rudiments of knowledge; precept after precept, line after line, here and there, by little and little? imitating at the same time, and ridiculing, in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.10">Isa 28:10</reference>, the concise prophetical manner. God, by his prophet, retorts upon them with great severity their own contemptuous mockery, turning it to a sense quite different from what they intended. Yes, saith he, it shall be in fact as you say; ye shall be taught by a strange tongue and a stammering lip; in a strange country; ye shall be carried into captivity by a people whose language shall be unintelligible to you, and which ye shall be forced to learn like children. And my dealing with you shall be according to your own words: it shall be command upon command for your punishment; it shall be line upon line, stretched over you to mark your destruction, (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.13">2Kgs 21:13</reference>); it shall come upon you at different times, and by different degrees, till the judgments, with which from time to time I have threatened you, shall have their full accomplishment. <div eID="gen27610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27611" type="x-p"/> Jerome seems to have rightly understood the general design of this passage as expressing the manner in which the scoffers, by their sententious speeches, turned into ridicule the warnings of God by his prophets, though he has not so well explained the meaning of the repetition of their speech in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.13">Isa 28:13</reference>. His words are on <reference osisRef="Isa.28.9">Isa 28:9</reference> "Solebant hoc ex persona prophetarum ludentes dicere:" and on <reference osisRef="Isa.28.14">Isa 28:14</reference> "Quod supra diximus, cum irrisione solitos principes Judaeorum prophetis dicere, manda, remanda, et caetera his similia, per quae ostenditur, nequaquam eos prophetarum credidisse sermonibus, sed prophetiam habuisse despectui, praesens ostendit capitulum, per quod appellantur viri illusores." Hieron. in loc. <div eID="gen27611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27612" type="x-p"/> And so Jarchi interprets the word משלים mishelim in the next verse: Qui dicunt verba irrisionis parabolice." And the Chaldee paraphrases <reference osisRef="Isa.28.11">Isa 28:11</reference> to the same purpose, understanding it as spoken, not of God, but of the people deriding his prophets: "Quoniam in mutatione loquelae et in lingua subsannationis irridebant contra prophetas, qui prophetabant populo huic." - L.
entries.779451ced74fa7b501fe64a2a7f5598277149281: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen27612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27613" type="x-p"/> For precept must be upon precept - The original is remarkably abrupt and sententious. The hemistichs are these: - לצו צו לצו צו כי latsav tsav latsav tsav ki לקו קו לקו קו lakau kau lakau kau שם זעיר שם זעיר sham zeeir sham zeeir <div eID="gen27613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27614" type="x-p"/> For, - Command to command, command to command. <div eID="gen27614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27615" type="x-p"/> Line to line, line to line. <div eID="gen27615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27616" type="x-p"/> A little there, a little there. <div eID="gen27616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27617" type="x-p"/> Kimchi says צו tsau, precept, is used here for מצוה mitsuah, command, and is used in no other place for it but here. צו tsau signifies a little precept, such as is suited to the capacity of a child; see <reference osisRef="Isa.28.9">Isa 28:9</reference>. קו kau signifies the line that a mason stretches out to build a layer of stones by. After one layer or course is placed, he raises the line and builds another; thus the building is by degrees regularly completed. This is the method of teaching children, giving them such information as their narrow capacities can receive; and thus the prophet dealt with the Israelites. See Kimchi in loc., and see a fine parallel passage, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.12-Heb.5.14">Heb 5:12-14</reference>, by which this may be well illustrated. <div eID="gen27617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27618" type="x-p"/> My old MS. Bible translates oddly: - <div eID="gen27618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27619" type="x-p"/> For sende efter sende, sende efter sende: <div eID="gen27619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27620" type="x-p"/> Abide efter abiide, abide efter abiide: <div eID="gen27620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27621" type="x-p"/> Lytyl ther, lytyl ther. <div eID="gen27621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27622" type="x-p"/> Coverdale is also singular: - <div eID="gen27622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27623" type="x-p"/> Commande that may be commanded; <div eID="gen27623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27624" type="x-p"/> Byd that maye be bydden: <div eID="gen27624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27625" type="x-p"/> Foorbyd that maye be forbydden; <div eID="gen27625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27626" type="x-p"/> Kepe backe that maye be kepte backe: <div eID="gen27626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27627" type="x-p"/> Here a litle, there a litle.
entries.ddef447aa9411a10fba6bc1245420678f0e06a14: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen27627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27628" type="x-p"/> This is the rest "This is the true rest" - The sense of this verse is: God had warned them by his prophets that their safety and security, their deliverance from their present calamities and from the apprehensions of still greater approaching, depended wholly on their trust in God, their faith and obedience; but they rejected this gracious warning with contempt and mockery.
entries.61f55a52180007e4462dc9c42b1db30ccfb82f48: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen27628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27629" type="x-p"/> A covenant with death - To be in covenant with, is a kind of proverbial expression to denote perfect security from evil and mischief of any sort: - "For thou shalt be in league with the stones of the field; <div eID="gen27629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27630" type="x-p"/> And the beasts of the field shall be at peace with thee." <reference osisRef="Job.5.23">Job 5:23</reference>. "And I will make a covenant for them with the beasts of the field. And with the fowls of heaven, and with the creeping things of the ground." <reference osisRef="Hos.2.18">Hos 2:18</reference>. <div eID="gen27630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27631" type="x-p"/> That is, none of these shall hurt them. But Lucan, speaking of the Psylli, whose peculiar property it was to be unhurt by the bite of serpents, with which their country abounded, comes still nearer to the expression of Isaiah in this place: - <div eID="gen27631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27632" type="x-p"/> Gens unica terras <div eID="gen27632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27633" type="x-p"/> Incolit a saevo serpentum innoxia morsu <div eID="gen27633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27634" type="x-p"/> Marmaridae Psylli. - <div eID="gen27634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27635" type="x-p"/> Pax illis cum morte data est. <div eID="gen27635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27636" type="x-p"/> Pharsal. 9:891. "Of all who scorching Afric's sun endure, <div eID="gen27636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27637" type="x-p"/> None like the swarthy Psyllians are secure: <div eID="gen27637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27638" type="x-p"/> With healing gifts and privileges graced, <div eID="gen27638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27639" type="x-p"/> Well in the land of serpents were they placed: <div eID="gen27639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27640" type="x-p"/> Truce with the dreadful tyrant death they have, <div eID="gen27640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27641" type="x-p"/> And border safely on his realm the grave." <div eID="gen27641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27642" type="x-p"/> Rowe. <div eID="gen27642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27643" type="x-p"/> We have made a covenant with death and with hell are we at agreement - עשינו חזה asinu chozeh, we have made a vision, we have had an interview, struck a bargain, and settled all preliminaries. So they had made a covenant with hell by diabolic sacrifice, כרתנו ברית carathnu beritth. "We have cut the covenant sacrifice;" they divided it for the contracting parties to pass between the separated victim; for the victim was split exactly down the middle, so that even the spinal marrow was exactly divided through its whole length; and being set opposite to each other, the contracting parties entered, one at the head part, the other at the feet; and, meeting in the center, took the covenant oath. Thus, it is intimated, these bad people made an agreement with שאול sheol, with demons, with whom they had an interview; i.e., meeting them in the covenant sacrifice! To such a pitch had the Israelitish idolatry reached at that time!
entries.4d47621ce9707cd18e445d20bbe723064efc3ea1: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen27643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27644" type="x-p"/> Behold, I lay in Zion - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.49.32">Gen 49:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Mat.21.42">Mat 21:42</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Act.4.11">Act 4:11</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Rom.9.33">Rom 9:33</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Rom.10.11">Rom 10:11</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Eph 2:20</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.6-1Pet.2.8">1Pet 2:6-8</reference> (note). Kimchi understands this of Hezekiah; but it most undoubtedly belongs to Jesus Christ alone; and his application of it to himself, even the Jews could not contest.
entries.4875e8dd7fb7d5f0b113f259ee98164836728f57: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen27644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27645" type="x-p"/> Your covenant with death shall be disannulled "Your covenant with death shall be broken" - For כפר caphar, which seems not to belong to this place, the Chaldee reads תפר taphar, which is approved by Houbigant and Secker. See <reference osisRef="Jer.33.21">Jer 33:21</reference>, where the very same phrase is used. See Prelim. Dissert. p. l.
entries.f47cf160c4b74e721ae9f22b963a37fd38b67060: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen27645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27646" type="x-p"/> For the bed is shorter - A mashal or proverbial saying, the meaning of which is, that they will find all means of defense and protection insufficient to secure them, and cover them from the evils coming upon them. מסך massek, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.8">Isa 22:8</reference>, the covering, is used for the outworks of defense, the barrier of the country; and here, in the allegorical sense, it means much the same thing. Their beds were only mattresses laid on the floor; and the coverlet a sheet, or in the winter a carpet, laid over it, in which the person wrapped himself. For כהתכנס kehithcannes, it ought probably to be מהתכנס mehithcannes. Houbigant, Secker.
entries.9a3767cc3a1a6c5a2505ed098bc282f50c031cb2: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen27646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27647" type="x-p"/> As in Mount Perazim - כהר kehar; but בהר bahar, In the mount, is the reading of two of Kennicott's, one of De Rossi's, and one of my own MSS.
entries.2d3f570e5f611a554f6a48fab35b8f2a37941a11: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen27647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27648" type="x-p"/> The Lord God - אדני יהוה Adonai Jehovah. Adonai is omitted by four of Kennicott's MSS., and in the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic.
entries.ae70aba88aed8b69d30361ebe24e65b1ef16bcb7: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen27648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27649" type="x-p"/> Give ye ear, and hear my voice "Listen ye, and hear my voice" - The foregoing discourse, consisting of severe reproofs, and threatenings of dreadful judgments impending on the Jews for their vices, and their profane contempt of God's warnings by his messengers, the prophet concludes with an explanation and defense of God's method of dealing with his people in an elegant parable or allegory; in which he employs a variety of images, all taken from the science of agriculture. As the husbandman uses various methods in preparing his land, and adapting it to the several kinds of seeds to be sown, with a due observation of times and seasons; and when he hath gathered in his harvest, employs methods as various in separating the corn from the straw and the chaff by different instruments, according to the nature of the different sorts of grain; so God, with unerring wisdom, and with strict justice, instructs, admonishes, and corrects his people; chastises and punishes them in various ways, as the exigence of the case requires; now more moderately, now more severely; always tempering justice with mercy; in order to reclaim the wicked, to improve the good, and, finally, to separate the one from the other.
entries.d9222d246b59c5c0df1f9a5de56c88794be22357: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen27649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27650" type="x-p"/> For his God doth instruct him - All nations have agreed in attributing agriculture, the most useful and the most necessary of all sciences, to the invention and to the suggestions of their deities. "The Most High hath ordained husbandry, "saith the son of Sirach, Ecclus. 7:15. <div eID="gen27650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27651" type="x-p"/> Namque Ceres fertur fruges, Liberque liquoris <div eID="gen27651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27652" type="x-p"/> Vitigeni laticem mortalibus instituisse. <div eID="gen27652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27653" type="x-p"/> Lucretius, 5:14. "Ceres has taught mortals how to produce fruits; and Bacchus has taught them how to cultivate the vine." Ὁ δ' ηπιος ανθρωποισι Δεξια σημαινει, λαους δ' επι εργον εγειρει Μιμνησκων βιοτοιο· λεγει δ' ὁτε βωλος αριστη Βουσι τε και μακελῃσι· λεγει δ' ὁτε δεξιαι ὡραι Και φυτα γυρωσαι, και σπερματα παντα βαλεσθαι. <div eID="gen27653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27654" type="x-p"/> Aratus, Phantom. v. "He, Jupiter, to the human race <div eID="gen27654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27655" type="x-p"/> Indulgent, prompts to necessary toil <div eID="gen27655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27656" type="x-p"/> Man provident of life; with kindly signs <div eID="gen27656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27657" type="x-p"/> The seasons marks, when best to turn the glebe <div eID="gen27657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27658" type="x-p"/> With spade and plough, to nurse the tender plant, <div eID="gen27658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27659" type="x-p"/> And cast o'er fostering earth the seeds abroad."
entries.261725bb614b49f603761af966ecd989b758aa71: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen27659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27660" type="x-p"/> Four methods of threshing are here mentioned, by different instruments; the flail, the drag, the wain, and the treading of the cattle. The staff or flail was used for the infirmiora semina, says Jerome, the grain that was too tender to be treated in the other methods. The drag consisted of a sort of strong planks, made rough at the bottom, with hard stones or iron; it was drawn by horses or oxen over the corn sheaves spread on the floor, the driver sitting upon it. Kempfer has given a print representing the manner of using this instrument, Amaen. Exot. p. 682, fig. 3. The wain was much like the former; but had wheels with iron teeth, or edges like a saw: Ferrata carpenta rotis per medium in serrarum modum se volventibus. Hieron. in loc. From this it would seem that the axle was armed with iron teeth or serrated wheels throughout. See a description and print of such a machine used at present in Egypt for the same purpose in Niebuhr's Voyage en Arabie, Tab. 17 p. 123; it moves upon three rollers armed with iron teeth or wheels to cut the straw. In Syria they make use of the drag, constructed in the very same manner as above described; Niebuhr, Description de l'Arabie, p. 140. This not only forced out the grain, but cut the straw in pieces for fodder for the cattle; for in the eastern countries they have no hay. See Harmer's Observ. 1 p. 425. The last method is well known from the law of Moses, which "forbids the ox to be muzzled, when he treadeth out the corn;" <reference osisRef="Deu.25.4">Deu 25:4</reference>.
entries.068458dd0b878cc3ae8144e47be27f8167a066fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen27660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27661" type="x-p"/> The bread-corn - I read ולהם velahem, on the authority of the Vulgate and Symmachus; the former expresses the conjunction ו vau, omitted in the text, by autem; the latter by δε. <div eID="gen27661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27662" type="x-p"/> Bruise it with his horsemen "Bruise it with the hoofs of his cattle" - For פרשיו parashaiv, horsemen or teeth, read פרסיו perasaiv, hoofs. So the Syriac, Syrnmachus, Theodotion, and the Vulgate. The first is read with ש shin, the latter with ס samech, the pronunciation is nearly the same.  <chapter eID="Isa.28"/> <div eID="gen27662" type="x-p"/>

entries.3fbf27996e9722ab7c4728d6d405e3fbcaf7698b: <div eID="gen13163" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Book of Woes or Historical Discourses Relating to Asshur and the Egyptian Alliance - Isaiah 28-33 part v</title> <div sID="gen13164" type="x-p"/> These chapters carry us to the earliest years of Hezekiah’s reign, probably to the second and third; as Samaria has not yet been destroyed. They run parallel to the book of Micah, which also takes its start from the destruction of Samaria, and are as faithful a mirror of the condition of the people under Hezekiah, as chapters 7-12 were of their condition under Ahaz. The time of Ahaz was characterized by a spiritless submission to the Assyrian yoke; that of Hezekiah by a casual striving after liberty. The people tried to throw off the yoke of Assyria; not with confidence in Jehovah, however, but in reliance upon the help of Egypt. This Egypticizing policy is traced step by step by Isaiah, in chapters 28-32. The gradual rise of these addresses may be seen from the fact, that they follow the gradual growth of the alliance with Egypt through all its stages, until it is fully concluded. By the side of this casual ground of trust, which Jehovah will sweep away, the prophet exhibits the precious corner-stone in Zion as the true, firm ground of confidence. We might therefore call these chapters (Isaiah 28-33) “the book of the precious corner-stone,” just as we called chapters 7-12 “the book of Immanuel.” But the prophecy in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa 28:16</reference> does not determine and mould the whole of this section, in the same manner in which the other section is moulded and governed by the prophecy of the Son of the Virgin. We therefore prefer to call this cycle of prophecy “the book of woes;” for censure and threatening are uttered here in repeated utterances of “<hi type="italic">woe</hi>,” not against Israel only, but more especially against Judah and Jerusalem, until at last, in chapter 33, the “<hi type="italic">hoi</hi> concerning Jerusalem” is changed into a “<hi type="italic">hoi</hi> concerning Asshur.” All the independent and self-contained addresses in this cycle of prophecy commence with <hi type="italic">hoi</hi> (“<hi type="italic">woe:</hi>” chapters 28, 29, 30, 31-32, 33). The section which does not begin with <hi type="italic">hoi</hi> (viz., <reference osisRef="Isa.32.9-Isa.32.20">Isa 32:9-20</reference>) is the last and dependent part of the long address commencing with Isa 31:1. On the other hand, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.15-Isa.29.24">Isa 29:15-24</reference> also commences with <hi type="italic">hoi</hi>, though it does not form a distinct address in itself, since chapter 29 forms a complete whole. The subdivisions of the sections, therefore, have not a uniform commencement throughout; but the separate and independent addresses all commence with <hi type="italic">hoi</hi>. The climax of these prophecies of woe is chapter 30. Up to this point the exclamation of woe gradually ascends, but in chapters 31-32 it begins to fall; and in chapter 33 (which contains an epilogue that was only added in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah’s reign) it has changed into the very opposite. The prophet begins with <hi type="italic">hoi</hi>, but it is a woe concerning the devastator. This <hi type="italic">utmost</hi> woe, however, was not fulfilled at the point of time when the fulfilment of “the utmost” predicted in chapters 28-32 was apparently close at hand; but Jerusalem, though threatened with destruction, was miraculously saved. Yet the prophet had not merely to look on, as Jonah had. He himself predicted this change in the purpose of God, inasmuch as the direction of the “woe” in his mouth is altered, like that of the wrath of God, which turns from Jerusalem to Asshur, and destroys it. <div eID="gen13164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13165" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">Isa 28:1</reference> <div eID="gen13165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13166" type="x-p"/> Isaiah, like Micah, commences with the fall of the proud and intoxicated Samaria. <hi type="italic">“Woe to the proud crown of the drunken of Ephraim, and to the fading flower of its splendid ornament, which is upon the head of the luxuriant valley of those slain with wine.”</hi> The allusion is to Samaria, which is called (1.) “the pride-crown of the drunken of Ephraim,” i.e., the crown of which the intoxicated and blinded Ephraimites were proud (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.9">Isa 29:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.14">Isa 19:14</reference>), and (2.) “the fading flower” (on the expression itself, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.30">Isa 1:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.7-Isa.40.8">Isa 40:7-8</reference>) “of the ornament of his splendour,” i.e., the flower now fading, which had once been the ornament with which they made a show. This flower stood “upon the head of the valley of fatnesses of those slain with wine” (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8">Isa 16:8</reference>), i.e., of the valley so exuberant with fruitfulness, belonging to the Ephraimites, who were thoroughly enslaved by wine. Samaria stood upon a beautiful swelling hill, which commanded the whole country round in a most regal way (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.1">Amo 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Amo 6:1</reference>), in the centre of a large basin, of about two hours’ journey in diameter, shut in by a gigantic circle of still loftier mountains (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.9">Amo 3:9</reference>). The situation was commanding; the hill terraced up to the very top; and the surrounding country splendid and fruitful (Ritter, <hi type="italic">Erdkunde</hi>, xvi. 660, 661). The expression used by the prophet is intentionally bombastic. He heaps genitives upon genitives, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">Isa 10:12</reference>; Isa 21:17. The words are linked together in pairs. <hi type="italic">Shemânı̄m</hi> (fatnesses) has the absolute form, although it is annexed to the following word, the logical relation overruling the syntactical usage (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.32.13">Isa 32:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.13">1Ch 9:13</reference>). The <hi type="italic">sesquipedalia verba</hi> are intended to produce the impression of excessive worldly luxuriance and pleasure, upon which the woe is pronounced. The epithet <hi type="italic">nōbhēl</hi> (fading: possibly a genitive, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.4">Isa 28:4</reference>), which is introduced here into the midst of this picture of splendour, indicates that all this splendour is not only destined to fade, but is beginning to fade already.
entries.d3a0ffc920852c47c6af195cecba7cea6f4ef71e: <reference osisRef="Isa.28.2-Isa.28.4">Isa 28:2-4</reference> <div eID="gen13166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13167" type="x-p"/> In the next three vv. the hoi is expanded. <hi type="italic">“Behold, the Lord holds a strong and mighty thing like a hailstorm, a pestilent tempest; like a storm of mighty overflowing waters, He casts down to the earth with almighty hand. With feet they tread down the proud crown of the drunken of Ephraim. And it happens to the fading flower of its splendid ornament, which is upon the head of the luxuriant valley, as to an early fig before it is harvest, which whoever sees it looks at, and it is no sooner in his hand than he swallows it.”</hi> “A strong and mighty thing:” ואמּי חזק we have rendered in the neuter (with the lxx and Targum) rather than in the masculine, as Luther does, although the strong and mighty thing which the Lord holds in readiness is no doubt the Assyrian. He is simply the medium of punishment in the hand of the Lord, which is called <hi type="italic">yâd</hi> absolutely, because it is absolute in power - as it were, the hand of all hands. This hand hurls Samaria to the ground (on the expression itself, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.25.12">Isa 25:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.5">Isa 26:5</reference>), so that they tread the proud crown to pieces with their feet (<hi type="italic">tērâmasnâh</hi>, the more pathetic plural form, instead of the singular <hi type="italic">tērâmēs</hi>; Ges. 47, Anm. 3, and Caspari on Oba 1:13). The noun <hi type="italic">sa‛ar</hi>, which is used elsewhere in the sense of shuddering, signifies here, like סערה, an awful tempest; and when connected with קטב, a tempest accompanied with a pestilential blast, spreading miasma. Such destructive power is held by the absolute hand. It is soon all over then with the splendid flower that has already begun to fade נבל ציצת, like הקּטן כּלי in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.24">Isa 22:24</reference>). It happens to it as to a <hi type="italic">bikkūrâh</hi> (according to the Masora, written with <hi type="italic">mappik</hi> here, as distinguished from Hos 9:10, equivalent to <hi type="italic">kebhikkūrâthâh</hi>; see <reference osisRef="Job.11.9">Job 11:9</reference>, “like an early fig of this valley;” according to others, it is simply euphonic). The gathering of figs takes place about August. Now, if any one sees a fig as early as June, he fixes his eyes upon it, and hardly touches it with his hand before he swallows it, and that without waiting to masticate it long. Like such a dainty bit will the luxuriant Samaria vanish. The fact that Shalmanassar, or his successor Sargon, did not conquer Samaria till after the lapse of three years (2Ki 18:10), does not detract from the truth of the prophecy; it is enough that both the thirst of the conqueror and the utter destruction of Samaria answered to it.
entries.26d5f3e4dbdcb96770986ccbda71b7f0e03340f2: <reference osisRef="Isa.28.5-Isa.28.6">Isa 28:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen13167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13168" type="x-p"/> The threat is now followed by a promise. This is essentially the same in character as <reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">Isa 4:2</reference>-6. The place of the false glory thus overthrown is now filled by a glory that is divine and true. <hi type="italic">“In that day will Jehovah of hosts be the adorning crown and the splendid diadem to the remnant of His people; and the spirit of justice to them that sit on the judgment-seat, and heroic strength to them that drive back war at the gate.”</hi> “The remnant of His people” (שׁאר with a fixed <hi type="italic">kametz</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.21.17">Isa 21:17</reference>) is not Judah, as distinguished from Ephraim that had utterly perished; but Judah and the remaining portion of Ephraim, as distinguished from the portion which had perished. After the perishable thin in which they gloried had been swept away, the eternal person of Jehovah Himself would be the ornament and pride of His people. He, the Lord of the seven spirits (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Isa 11:1</reference>), would be to this remnant of His people the spirit of right and heroic strength. There would be an end to unjust judging and powerless submission. The judges are called “those who sit <hi type="italic">‛al</hi>-<hi type="italic">hammishpât</hi>” in the sense of “on the seat of judgment” (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.5">Psa 9:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.122.5">Psa 122:5</reference>); the warriors are called “those who press back <hi type="italic">milchâmâh</hi> <hi type="italic">shâ‛râh</hi>” (war at the gate), i.e., either war that has reached their own gate (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.7">Isa 22:7</reference>), or war which they drive back as far as the gate of the enemy (<reference osisRef="2Sam.11.23">2Sa 11:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.1">1</reference> Macc. 5:22). The promise in this last passage corresponds to Mic 5:4-5. The <hi type="italic">athnach</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.6">Isa 28:6</reference> ought to stand at <hi type="italic">hammishpât</hi>; the second clause of the v. may be completed from the first, ולגבוּרה being equivalent to גבורה ולרוח, and משיבי to למישבי. We might regard 2 Chron 30 as a fulfilment of what is predicted in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.6">Isa 28:6</reference>, if the feast of passover there described really fell in the age succeeding the fall of Samaria; for this feast of passover did furnish a representation and awaken a consciousness of that national unity which had been interrupted from the time of Rehoboam. But if we read the account in the Chronicles with unprejudiced minds, it is impossible to shut our eyes to the fact that this feast of passover took place in the second month of the first year of Hezekiah’s reign, and therefore not after the depopulation of the northern kingdom by Shalmanassar, but after the previous and partial depopulation by Tiglath-pileser. In fact, the fulfilment cannot be looked for at all in the space between the sixth and fourteenth years of Hezekiah, since the condition of Judah during that time does not answer at all to the promises given above. The prophet here foretells what might be hoped for, when Asshur had not only humbled Ephraim, but Judah also. The address consists of two connected halves, the promising beginnings of which point to one and the same future, and lay hold of one another.
entries.cc7fca70f09952e8eb2b44c4bb43c60bbf97109e: <reference osisRef="Isa.28.7-Isa.28.8">Isa 28:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen13168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13169" type="x-p"/> With the words, “and they also,” the prophet commences the second half of the address, and passes from Ephraim to Judah. <hi type="italic">“And they also reel with wine, and are giddy with meth; priest and prophet reel with meth, are swallowed up by wine: they are giddy with meth, reel when seeing visions, stagger when pronouncing judgment. For all tables are full of filthy vomit, without any more place.”</hi> The Judaeans are not less overcome with wine than the Ephraimites, and especially the rulers of Judah. In wicked violation of the law of God, which prohibited the priests from drinking strong drink when performing priestly service, and that on pain of death (<reference osisRef="Lev.10.9">Lev 10:9</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.21">Eze 44:21</reference>), they were intoxicated even in the midst of their prophetic visions (הראה, literally “the thing seeing,” then the act of seeing; equivalent to ראי, like חזה in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.15">Isa 28:15</reference> = חזוּת; Olshausen, §176,<hi type="italic">c</hi>), and when passing judicial sentences. In the same way Micah also charges the prophets and priests with being drunkards (Mic 3:1., cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">Isa 2:11</reference>). Isaiah’s indignation is manifested in the fact, that in the words which he uses he imitates the staggering and stumbling of the topers; like the well-known passage, <hi type="italic">Sta pes sta mi pes stas pes ne labere mi pes</hi>. Observe, for example, the threefold repetition of <hi type="italic">shâgu</hi> - <hi type="italic">tâghu</hi>, <hi type="italic">shâgu</hi> - <hi type="italic">tâghu</hi>, <hi type="italic">shâgu</hi> - <hi type="italic">pâqu</hi>. The hereditary priests and the four prophets represent the whole of the official personages. The preterites imply that drunkenness had become the fixed habit of the holders of these offices. The preposition בּ indicates the cause (“through,” as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.13.28">2Sa 13:28</reference> and <reference osisRef="Esth.1.10">Est 1:10</reference>), and <hi type="italic">min</hi> the effect proceeding from the cause (in consequence of wine). In v. 8 we can hear them vomit. We have the same combination of the and צ in the verb <hi type="italic">kotzen</hi>, Gothic <hi type="italic">kozan</hi>. All the tables of the carousal are full, without there being any further room (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">Isa 5:8</reference>); everything swims with vomit. The prophet paints from nature, here without idealizing. He receives their conduct as it were in a mirror, and then in the severest tones holds up this mirror before them, adults though they were.
entries.263dd237a46e9ece717b1f3f8bfa57d10cc57c1a: <reference osisRef="Isa.28.9-Isa.28.10">Isa 28:9-10</reference> <hi type="italic">“Whom then would he teach knowledge? And to whom make preaching intelligible? To those weaned from the milk? To those removed from the breast? For precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, a little here, a little there!”</hi> They sneer at the prophet, that intolerable moralist. They are of age, and free; and he does not need to bring knowledge to them (<hi type="italic">da‛ath</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Isa.11.9">Isa 11:9</reference>), or make them understand the proclamation. They know of old to what he would lead. Are they little children that have just been weaned (on the constructives, see <reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">Isa 9:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.11">Isa 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.18">Isa 30:18</reference>; Ges. §114, 1), and who must let themselves be tutored? For the things he preaches are nothing but endless petty teazings. The short words (<hi type="italic">tsâv</hi>, as in Hos 5:11), together with the diminutive זעיר (equivalent to the Arabic <hi type="italic">sugayyir</hi>, mean, from <hi type="italic">sagı̄r</hi>, small), are intended to throw ridicule upon the smallness and vexatious character of the prophet’s interminable and uninterrupted chidings, as ל (= על, אל; comp. יסף ל, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.15">Isa 26:15</reference>) implies that they are; just as the philosophers in <reference osisRef="Acts.17.18">Act 17:18</reference> call Paul a σπερμολόγος, a collector of seeds, i.e., a dealer in trifles. And in the repetition of the short words we may hear the heavy babbling language of the drunken scoffers.
entries.9b58c19c25793cb1e52d273e9ed721af03912b7f: <reference osisRef="Isa.28.11-Isa.28.13">Isa 28:11-13</reference> <div eID="gen13169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13170" type="x-p"/> The prophet takes the <hi type="italic">ki</hi> (“for”) out of their mouths, and carries it on in his own way. It was quite right that their ungodliness should show itself in such a way as this, for it would meet with an appropriate punishment. <hi type="italic">“For through men stammering in speech, and through a strange tongue, will He speak to this people. He who said to them, There is rest, give rest to weary ones, and there is refreshing! But they would not hear. Therefore the word of Jehovah becomes to them precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, a little here, a little there, that they may go and stumble backwards, and be wrecked to pieces, and be snared and taken.”</hi> Jehovah would speak to the scoffing people of stammering tongue a language of the same kind, since He would speak to them by a people that stammered in their estimation, i.e., who talked as barbarians (cf., βαρβαρίζειν and <hi type="italic">balbutire</hi>; see <reference osisRef="Isa.33.19">Isa 33:19</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Deut.28.49">Deu 28:49</reference>). The Assyrian Semitic had the same sound in the ear of an Israelite, as Low Saxon (a provincial dialect) in the ear of an educated German; in addition to which, it was plentifully mixed up with Iranian, and possibly also with Tatar elements. This people would practically interpret the will of Jehovah in its own <hi type="italic">patios</hi> to the despisers of the prophet. Jehovah had directed them, through His prophets, after the judgments which they had experienced with sufficient severity (Isa 1:5.), into the true way to rest and refreshing (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jer 6:16</reference>), and had exhorted them to give rest to the nation, which had suffered so much under Ahaz through the calamities of war (2 Chron 28), and not to drag it into another way by goading it on to rise against Assyria, or impose a new burden in addition to the tribute to Assyria by purchasing the help of Egypt. But they would not hearken (אבוּא = אבוּ, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.15-Isa.30.16">Isa 30:15-16</reference>; Ges. §23, 3, Anm. 3). Their policy was a very different one from being still, or believing and waiting. And therefore the word of Jehovah, which they regarded as en endless series of trivial commands, would be turned in their case into an endless series of painful sufferings. To those who thought themselves so free, and lived so free, it would become a stone on which they would go to pieces, a net in which they would be snared, a trap in which they would be caught (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.8.14-Isa.8.15">Isa 8:14-15</reference>).
entries.b945145eca6a813e841f081b9e0cb0754a2d916b: <reference osisRef="Isa.28.14-Isa.28.17">Isa 28:14-17</reference> <div eID="gen13170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13171" type="x-p"/> The prophet now directly attacks the great men of Jerusalem, and holds up a Messianic prophecy before their eyes, which turns its dark side to them, as chapter 7 did to Ahaz. <hi type="italic">“Therefore hear the word of Jehovah, ye scornful lords, rulers of this people which is in Jerusalem! For ye say, We have made a covenant with death, and with Hades have we come to an agreement. The swelling scourge, when it cometh hither, will do us no harm; for we have made a lie our shelter, and in deceit have we hidden ourselves. Therefore thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Behold, I am He who hath laid in Zion a stone, a stone of trial, a precious corner-stone of well-founded founding; whoever believes will not have to move. And I make justice the line, and righteousness the level; and hail sweeps away the refuge of lies, and the hiding-place is washed away by waters.”</hi> With <hi type="italic">lâkhēn</hi> (therefore) the announcement of punishment is once more suspended; and in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa 28:16</reference> it is resumed again, the exposition of the sin being inserted between, before the punishment is declared. Their sin is <hi type="italic">lâtsōn</hi>, and this free-thinking scorn rests upon a proud and insolent self-confidence, which imagines that there is no necessity to fear death and hell; and this self-confidence has for its secret reserve the alliance to be secretly entered into with Egypt against Assyria. What the prophet makes them say here, they do not indeed say exactly in this form; but this is the essential substance of the carnally devised thoughts and words of the rulers of the people of Jerusalem, as manifest to the Searcher of hearts. Jerusalem, the city of Jehovah, and such princes as these, who either proudly ignore Jehovah, or throw Him off as useless, what a contrast! <hi type="italic">Chōzeh</hi>, and <hi type="italic">châzūth</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.18">Isa 28:18</reference>, signify an agreement, either as a decision or completion (from the radical meaning of the verb <hi type="italic">châzâh</hi>), or as a choice, <hi type="italic">beneplacitum</hi> (like the Arabic <hi type="italic">ray</hi>), or as a record, i.e., the means of selecting (like the talmudic <hi type="italic">châzı̄th</hi>, a countersign, a <hi type="italic">ra'ăyâh</hi>, a proof or argument: Luzzatto). In <hi type="italic">shōt</hi> <hi type="italic">shōtēph</hi> (“the swelling scourge,” <hi type="italic">chethib</hi> שׁיט), the comparison of Asshur to a flood (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.2">Isa 28:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.8">Isa 28:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.7">Isa 28:7</reference>), and the comparison of it to a whip or scourge, are mixed together; and this is all the more allowable, because a whip, when smacked, really does move in waving lines (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.8.6">Jer 8:6</reference>, where <hi type="italic">shâtaph</hi> is applied to the galloping of a war-horse). The <hi type="italic">chethib</hi> עבר in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.15">Isa 28:15</reference> (for which the <hi type="italic">keri</hi> reads יעבר, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.28.19">Isa 28:19</reference>) is to be read עבר (granting that it shall have passed, or that it passes); and there is no necessity for any emendation. The Egyptian alliance for which they are suing, when designated according to its true ethical nature, is <hi type="italic">sheqer</hi> (lie) and <hi type="italic">kâzâb</hi> (falsehood); compare 2Ki 17:4 (where we ought perhaps to read <hi type="italic">sheqer</hi> for <hi type="italic">qesher</hi>, according to the lxx), and more especially Eze 17:15., from which it is obvious that the true prophets regarded self-willed rebellion even against heathen rule as a reprehensible breach of faith. <div eID="gen13171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13172" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">lâkhēn</hi> (therefore), which is resumed in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa 28:16</reference>, is apparently followed as strangely as in <reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">Isa 7:14</reference>, by a promise instead of a threat. But this is only apparently the case. It is unquestionably a promise; but as the last clause, “he that believeth will not flee,” i.e., will stand firm, clearly indicates, it is a promise for believers alone. For those to whom the prophet is speaking here the promise is a threat, a savour of death unto death. Just as on a former occasion, when Ahaz refused to ask for a sign, the prophet announced to him a sign of Jehovah’s own selection; so here Jehovah opposes to the false ground of confidence on which the leaders relied, the foundation stone laid in Zion, which would bear the believing in immoveable safety, but on which the unbelieving would be broken to pieces (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.44">Mat 21:44</reference>). This stone is called <hi type="italic">'ebhen</hi> boochan, a stone of proving, i.e., a proved and self-proving stone. Then follow other epithets in a series commencing anew with <hi type="italic">pinnath</hi> = <hi type="italic">'ebhen</hi> <hi type="italic">pinnath</hi> (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference>): <hi type="italic">angulus h. e. lapis angularis pretiositatis fundationis fundatae</hi>. It is a corner-stone, valuable in itself (on <hi type="italic">yiqrath</hi>, compare 1Ki 5:17), and affording the strongest foundation and inviolable security to all that is built upon it (<hi type="italic">mūsâd</hi> a substantive in form like <hi type="italic">mūsâr</hi>, and <hi type="italic">mūssâd</hi> a <hi type="italic">hophal</hi> participle in the form of those of the <hi type="italic">verba contracta pe yod</hi>). This stone was not the Davidic sovereignty, but the true seed of David which appeared in Jesus (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.33">Rom 9:33</reference>; 1Pe 2:6-7). The figure of a stone is not opposed to the personal reference, since the prophet in <reference osisRef="Isa.8.14">Isa 8:14</reference> speaks even of Jehovah Himself under the figure of a stone. The majestically unique description renders it quite impossible that Hezekiah can be intended. Micah, whose book forms the side piece of this cycle of prophecy, also predicted, under similar historical circumstances, the birth of the Messiah in Bethlehem Ephratah (Mic 5:1). What Micah expresses in the words, “His goings forth are from of old,” is indicated here in the preterite <hi type="italic">yissad</hi> connected with <hi type="italic">hineni</hi> (the construction is similar to that in Oba 1:2; <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.7">Eze 25:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.28.2">Isa 28:2</reference> above, and <reference osisRef="Jer.49.15">Jer 49:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.19">Jer 23:19</reference>). It denotes that which has been determined by Jehovah, and therefore is as good as accomplished. What is historically realized has had an eternal existence, and indeed an ideal pre-existence even in the heart of history itself (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa 22:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.1">Isa 25:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.26">Isa 37:26</reference>). Ever since there had been a Davidic government at all, this stone had lain in Zion. The Davidic monarchy not only had in this its culminating point, but the ground of its continuance also. It was not only the Omega, but also the Alpha. Whatever escaped from wrath, even under the Old Testament, stood upon this stone. This (as the prophet predicts in יסהישׁ לא המּאמין יחישׁ׃ the fut. <hi type="italic">kal</hi>) would be the stronghold of faith in the midst of the approaching Assyrian calamities (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.7.9">Isa 7:9</reference>); and faith would be the condition of life (<reference osisRef="Hab.2.4">Hab 2:4</reference>). But against unbelievers Jehovah would proceed according to His punitive justice. He would make this (justice and righteousness, <hi type="italic">mishpât</hi> and <hi type="italic">tsedâqâh</hi>) a norm, i.e., a line and level. A different turn, however, is given to <hi type="italic">qâv</hi>, with a play upon <reference osisRef="Isa.28.10">Isa 28:10</reference>, Isa 28:11. What Jehovah is about to do is depicted as a building which He is carrying out, and which He will carry out, so far as the despisers are concerned, on no other plan than that of strict retribution. His punitive justice comes like a hailstorm and like a flood (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.28.2">Isa 28:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.22">Isa 10:22</reference>). The hail smites the refuge of lies of the great men of Jerusalem, and clears it away (יעה, hence יע, a shovel); and the flood buries their hiding-place in the waters, and carries it away (the accentuation should be סתר <hi type="italic">tifchah</hi>, מים <hi type="italic">mercha</hi>).
entries.7304dbd643f30ab590c20149fa7a7428922ecbd2: <reference osisRef="Isa.28.18-Isa.28.20">Isa 28:18-20</reference> <div eID="gen13172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13173" type="x-p"/> And the whip which Jehovah swings will not be satisfied with one stroke, but will rain strokes. <hi type="italic">“And your covenant with death is struck out, and your agreement with Hades will not stand; the swelling scourge, when it comes, ye will become a thing trodden down to it. As often as it passes it takes you: for every morning it passes, by day and by night; and it is nothing but shuddering to hear such preaching. For the bed is too short to stretch in, and the covering too tight when a man wraps himself in it.”</hi> Although <hi type="italic">berı̄th</hi> is feminine, the predicate to it is placed before it in the masculine form (Ges. §144). The covenant is thought of as a document; for <hi type="italic">khuppar</hi> (for <hi type="italic">obliterari</hi> (just as the <hi type="italic">kal</hi> is used in <reference osisRef="Gen.6.14">Gen 6:14</reference> in the sense of <hi type="italic">oblinere</hi>; or in <reference osisRef="Prov.30.20">Pro 30:20</reference>, the Targum, and the Syriac, in the sense of <hi type="italic">abstergere</hi>; and in the Talmud frequently in the sense of wiping off = <hi type="italic">qinnēăch</hi>, or wiping out = <hi type="italic">mâchaq</hi> - which meanings all go back, along with the meaning <hi type="italic">negare</hi>, to the primary meaning, <hi type="italic">tegere</hi>, <hi type="italic">obducere</hi>). The covenant will be “struck out,” as you strike out a wrong word, by crossing it over with ink and rendering it illegible. They fancy that they have fortified themselves against death and Hades; but Jehovah gives to both of these unlimited power over them. When the swelling scourge shall come, they will become to it as <hi type="italic">mirmâs</hi>, i.e., they will be overwhelmed by it, and their corpses become like dirt of the streets (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">Isa 10:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.5">Isa 5:5</reference>); והייתם has the <hi type="italic">mercha</hi> upon the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>., according to the older editions and the smaller Masora on <reference osisRef="Lev.8.26">Lev 8:26</reference>, the tone being drawn back on account of the following לו. The strokes of the scourge come incessantly, and every stroke sweeps them, i.e., many of them, away. מדּי (from דּי, construct דּי, sufficiency, abundance) followed by the infinitive, <hi type="italic">quotiescunque irruet</hi>; <hi type="italic">lâqach</hi>, <hi type="italic">auferre</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.15.15">Jer 15:15</reference>, and in the idiom <hi type="italic">lâqach nephesh</hi>. These scourgings without end - what a painful lecture Jehovah is reading them! This is the thought expressed in the concluding words: for the meaning cannot be, that “even (<hi type="italic">raq</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Ps.32.6">Psa 32:6</reference>) the report (of such a fate) is alarming,” as Grotius and others explain it; or the report is nothing but alarming, as Gussetius and others interpret it, since in that case שׁמועה שׁמע (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.23.5">Isa 23:5</reference>) would have been quite sufficient, instead of שׁמוּעה הבין. There is no doubt that the expression points back to the scornful question addressed by the debauchees to the prophet in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.9">Isa 28:9</reference>, “To whom will he make preaching intelligible?” i.e., to whom will he preach the word of God in an intelligible manner? (as if they did not possess <hi type="italic">bı̄nâh</hi> without this; שׁמוּעה, ἀκοή, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.53.1">Isa 53:1</reference>). As <reference osisRef="Isa.28.11">Isa 28:11</reference> affirmed that Jehovah would take up the word against them, the drunken stammerers, through a stammering people; so here the scourging without end is called the <hi type="italic">shemū‛âh</hi>, or sermon, which Jehovah preaches to them. At the same time, the word <hi type="italic">hâbhı̄n</hi> is not causative here, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.9">Isa 28:9</reference>, viz., “to give to understand,” but signifies simply “to understand,” or have an inward perception. To receive into one’s comprehension such a sermon as that which was now being delivered to them, was <hi type="italic">raq</hi>-<hi type="italic">zevâ‛âh</hi>, nothing but shaking or shuddering (<hi type="italic">raq</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Gen.6.5">Gen 6:5</reference>); זוּע (from which comes זועה, or by transposition זעוה) is applied to inward shaking as well as to outward tossing to and fro. Jerome renders it “<hi type="italic">tantummodo sola vexatio intellectum dabit auditui</hi>,” and Luther follows him thus: “but the vexation teaches to take heed to the word,” as if the reading were תּבין. The alarming character of the lecture is depicted in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.20">Isa 28:20</reference>, in a figure which was probably proverbial. The situation into which they are brought is like a bed too short for a man to stretch himself in (<hi type="italic">min</hi> as in 2Ki 6:1), and like a covering which, according to the measure of the man who covers himself up in it (or perhaps still better in a temporal sense, “when a man covers or wraps himself up in it,” cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.18.4">Isa 18:4</reference>), is too narrow or too tight. So would it be in their case with the Egyptian treaty, in which they fancied that there were rest and safety for them. They would have to acknowledge its insufficiency. They had made themselves a bed, and procured bed-clothes; but how mistaken they had been in the measure, how miserably and ridiculously they had miscalculated!
entries.bf94e46f01d2a4d97529029760ab0c18cbb52140: <reference osisRef="Isa.28.21">Isa 28:21</reference> <div eID="gen13173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13174" type="x-p"/> It would be with them as it was with the Philistines when David turned their army into water at Baal-perazim (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.20">2Sa 5:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.14.11">1Ch 14:11</reference>), or when on another occasion he drove them before him from Gibeon to Gezer (1Ch 14:13.). <hi type="italic">“For Jehovah will rise up as in the mountain of Perazim, and be wroth as in the valley at Gibeon to work His work; astonishing is His work; and to act His act: strange is His act.”</hi> The Targum wrongly supposes the first historical reminiscence to refer to the earthquake in the time of Uzziah, and the second to Joshua’s victory over the Amorites. The allusion really is to the two shameful defeats which David inflicted upon the Philistines. There was a very good reason why victories over the Philistines especially should serve as similes. The same fate awaited the Philistines at the hands of the Assyrians, as predicted by the prophet in Isa 14:28. (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Isa 20:1-6</reference>). And the strangeness and verity of Jehovah’s work were just this, that it would fare no better with the magnates of Judah at the hand of Asshur, than it had with the Philistines at the hand of David on both those occasions. The very same thing would now happen to the people of the house of David as formerly to its foes. Jehovah would have to act in opposition to His gracious purpose. He would have to act towards His own people as He once acted towards their foes. This was the most paradoxical thing of all that they would have to experience.
entries.53e9db0602f5b2e55f1715a1af9fec55ad4119b8: <reference osisRef="Isa.28.22">Isa 28:22</reference> <div eID="gen13174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13175" type="x-p"/> But the possibility of repentance was still open to them, and at least a modification of what had been threatened was attainable. <hi type="italic">“And now drive ye not mockeries, lest your fetters be strengthened; for I have heard from the Lord, Jehovah of hosts, a judgment of destruction, and an irrevocable one, upon the whole earth.”</hi> It is assumed that they are already in fetters, namely, the fetters of Asshur (<reference osisRef="Nah.1.13">Nah 1:13</reference>). Out of these fetters they wanted to escape by a breach of faith, and with the help of Egypt without Jehovah, and consequently they mocked at the warnings of the prophet. He therefore appeals to them at any rate to stop their mocking, lest they should fall out of the bondage in which they now ere, into one that would bind them still more closely, and lest the judgment should become even more severe than it would otherwise be. For it was coming without fail. It might be modified, and with thorough repentance they might even escape; but that it would come, and that upon the whole earth, had been revealed to the prophet by Jehovah of hosts. This was the <hi type="italic">shemū‛âh</hi> which the prophet had heard from Jehovah, and which he gave them to hear and understand, though hitherto he had only been scoffed at by their wine-bibbing tongues.
entries.5e3244423e42ac7e4d606141d8a955030e866d8f: <reference osisRef="Isa.28.23-Isa.28.26">Isa 28:23-26</reference>  The address of the prophet is here apparently closed. But an essential ingredient is still wanting to the second half, to make it correspond to the first. There is still wanting the fringe of promise coinciding with <reference osisRef="Isa.28.5">Isa 28:5</reference>, Isa 28:6. The prophet has not only to alarm the scoffers, that if possible he may pluck some of them out of the fire through fear (Jdg 5:23); he has also to comfort believers, who yield themselves as disciples to him and to the word of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.16">Isa 8:16</reference>). He does this here in a very peculiar manner. He has several times assumed the tone of the <hi type="italic">mashal</hi>, more especially in chapter 26; but here the consolation is dressed up in a longer parabolical address, which sets forth in figures drawn from husbandry the disciplinary and saving wisdom of God. Isaiah here proves himself a master of the mashal. In the usual tone of a mashal song, he first of all claims the attention of his audience as a teacher of wisdom. V. 23 <hi type="italic">“Lend me your ear, and hear my voice; attend, and hear my address!”</hi> Attention is all the more needful, that the prophet leaves his hearers to interpret and apply the parable themselves. The work of a husbandman is very manifold, as he tills, sows, and plants his field. Vv. 24-26 <hi type="italic">“Does the ploughman plough continually to sow? to furrow and to harrow his land? Is it not so: when he levels the surface thereof, he scatters black poppy seed, and strews cummin, and puts in wheat in rows, and barley in the appointed piece, and spelt on its border? And He has instructed him how to act rightly: his God teaches it him.”</hi> The ploughing (<hi type="italic">chârash</hi>) which opens the soil, i.e., turns it up in furrows, and the harrowing (<hi type="italic">siddēd</hi>) which breaks the clods, take place to prepare for the sowing, and therefore not interminably, but only so long as it necessary to prepare the soil to receive the seed. When the seed-furrows have been drawn in the levelled surface of the ground (<hi type="italic">shivvâh</hi>), then the sowing and planting begin; and this also takes place in various ways, according to the different kinds of fruit. <hi type="italic">Qetsach</hi> is the black poppy (<hi type="italic">nigella sativa</hi>, Arab. <hi type="italic">habbe soda</hi>, so called from its black seeds), belonging to the <hi type="italic">ranunculaceae</hi>. <hi type="italic">Kammōn</hi> was the cummin (<hi type="italic">c uminum cyminum</hi>) with larger aromatic seeds, Ar. <hi type="italic">kammūn</hi>, neither of them our common carraway (<hi type="italic">Kümmel</hi>, <hi type="italic">carum</hi>). The wheat he sows carefully in rows (<hi type="italic">sōrâh</hi>, <hi type="italic">ordo</hi>; <hi type="italic">ad ordinem</hi>, as it is translated by Jerome), i.e., he does not scatter it about carelessly, like the other two, but lays the grains carefully in the furrows, because otherwise when they sprang up they would get massed together, and choke one another. <hi type="italic">Nismân</hi>, like <hi type="italic">sōrâh</hi>, is an <hi type="italic">acc. loci</hi>: the barley is sown in a piece of the field specially marked off for it, or specially furnished with signs (<hi type="italic">sı̄mânı̄m</hi>); and <hi type="italic">kussemeth</hi>, the spelt (ζειά, also mentioned by Homer, <hi type="italic">Od</hi>. iv 604, between wheat and barley), along the edge of it, so that spelt forms the rim of the barley field. It is by a divine instinct that the husbandman acts in this manner; for God, who established agriculture at the creation (i.e., Jehovah, not Osiris), has also given men understanding. This is the meaning of <hi type="italic">v'yisserō lammishpât</hi>: and (as we may see from all this) <hi type="italic">He</hi> (his God: the subject is given afterwards in the second clause) <hi type="italic">has led him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.1">Pro 31:1</reference>) <hi type="italic">to the right</hi> (this is the rendering adopted by Kimchi, whilst other commentators have been misled by <reference osisRef="Jer.30.11">Jer 30:11</reference>, and last of all Malbim Luzzatto, “<hi type="italic">Cosi Dio con giustizia corregge</hi>;” he would have done better, however, to say, <hi type="italic">con moderazione</hi>).
entries.be952b65d6d3c4c526056cdf1af65b4a24622ea4: <reference osisRef="Isa.28.27-Isa.28.29">Isa 28:27-29</reference> <div eID="gen13175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13176" type="x-p"/> Again, the labour of the husbandman is just as manifold after the reaping has been done. <hi type="italic">“For the black poppy is not threshed with a threshing sledge, nor is a cart wheel rolled over cummin; but black poppy is knocked out with a stick, and cummin with a staff. Is bread corn crushed? No; he does not go on threshing it for ever, and drive the wheel of his cart and his horses over it: he does not crush it. This also, it goeth forth from Jehovah of hosts: He gives wonderful intelligence, high understanding.”</hi> <hi type="italic">Ki</hi> (for) introduces another proof that the husbandman is instructed by God, from what he still further does. He does not use the threshing machine (<hi type="italic">chârūts</hi>, syn. <hi type="italic">mōrag</hi>, Ar. <hi type="italic">naureg</hi>, <hi type="italic">nōreg</hi>), or the threshing cart (<hi type="italic">agâlâh</hi>: see Winer’s <hi type="italic">Real-Wörterbuch</hi>, art. <hi type="italic">Dreschen</hi>), which would entirely destroy the more tender kinds of fruit, but knocks them out with a staff (<hi type="italic">baculo excutit</hi>: see at <reference osisRef="Isa.27.12">Isa 27:12</reference>). The sentence <hi type="italic">lechem yūdâq</hi> is to be accentuated as an interrogative: Is bread corn crushed? Oh no, he does not crush it. This would be the case if he were to cause the wheel (i.e., the wheels, <hi type="italic">gilgal</hi>, constr. to <hi type="italic">galgal</hi>) of the threshing cart with the horses harnessed in front to rattle over it with all their might (<hi type="italic">hâmam</hi>, to set in noisy violent motion). Lechem, like the Greek <hi type="italic">sitos</hi>, is corn from which bread is made (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.23">Isa 30:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.14">Psa 104:14</reference>). אדושׁ is metaplastic (as if from אדשׁ) for דושׁ (see Ewald, §312,<hi type="italic">b</hi>). Instead of וּפרשׁיו, the pointing ought to be וּפרשׁיו (from פרשׁ with <hi type="italic">kametz</hi> before the tone = Arab. <hi type="italic">faras</hi>, as distinguished from פרשׁ with a fixed <hi type="italic">kametz</hi>, equivalent to <hi type="italic">farras</hi>, a rider): “his horses,” here the threshing horses, which were preferred to asses and oxen.Even in this treatment of the fruit when reaped, there is an evidence of the <hi type="italic">wonderful intelligence</hi> (הפלא), as written הפלא) and <hi type="italic">exalted understanding</hi> (on תּוּשׁהיה, from ושׁי, see at <reference osisRef="Job.26.3">Job 26:3</reference>) imparted by God. The expression is one of such grandeur, that we perceive at once that the prophet has in his mind the wisdom of God in a higher sphere. The wise, divinely inspired course adopted by the husbandman in the treatment of the field and fruit, is a type of the wise course adopted by the divine Teacher Himself in the treatment of His nation. Israel is Jehovah’s field. The punishments and chastisements of Jehovah are the ploughshare and harrow, with which He forcibly breaks up, turns over, and furrows this field. But this does not last for ever. When the field has been thus loosened, smoothed, and rendered fertile once more, the painful process of ploughing is followed by a beneficent sowing and planting in a multiform and wisely ordered fulness of grace. Again, Israel is Jehovah’s child of the threshing-floor (see <reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">Isa 21:10</reference>). He threshes it; but He does not thresh it only: He also knocks; and when He threshes, He does not continue threshing for ever, i.e., as Caspari has well explained it, “He does not punish all the members of the nation with the same severity; and those whom He punishes with greater severity than others He does not punish incessantly, but as soon as His end is attained, and the husks of sin are separated from those that have been punished, and the punishment ceases, and only the worst in the nation, who are nothing but husks, and the husks on the nation itself, are swept away by the punishments” (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.25">Isa 1:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.20-Isa.29.21">Isa 29:20-21</reference>). This is the solemn lesson and affectionate consolation hidden behind the veil of the parable. Jehovah punishes, but it is in order that He may be able to bless. He sifts, but He does not destroy. He does not thresh His own people, but He knocks them; and even when He threshes, they may console themselves in the face of the approaching period of judgment, that they are never crushed or injured.  <chapter eID="Isa.28"/> <div eID="gen13176" type="x-p"/>

entries.ad4f51f0be68dde8f9e5d0fb64defe47f321e698: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.28.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.28.1" sID="gen44897" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44898" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">Woe to the crown of pride.</hi> Isaiah now enters on another and different subject from that which goes before it; for this discourse must be separated from the former one. He shews that the anger of the Lord will quickly overtake, first, Israel, and afterwards the Jews; for it is probable that the kingdom of Israel was still entire when the Prophet uttered these predictions, though nothing more can be affirmed with certainty than that there is good reason to believe that the ten tribes had not at that time been led into captivity.<div eID="gen44898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44899" type="x-p"/>Accordingly, the Prophet follows this order. First, he shews that the vengeance of God is not far from Israel, because various sins and corruption of every kind prevailed in it; for they were swelled with pride and insolence, had plunged into their luxuries and given way to every kind of licentiousness, and, consequently, had broken out into open contempt of God, as is usually the case when men take excessive liberties; for they quickly forget God. Secondly, he shews that God in some measure restrains his anger by sparing the tribe of Judah; for when the ten tribes, with the half tribe of Benjamin, had been carried into captivity, the Jews still remained entire and uninjured. Isaiah extols this compassion which God manifested, in not permitting his Church to perish, but preserving some remnant. At the same time he shews that the Jews are so depraved and corrupted that they do not permit God to exercise this compassion, and that, in consequence of the wickedness which prevailed among them, not less than in Israel, they too must feel the avenging hand of God. This order ought to be carefully observed; for many persons blunder in the exposition of this passage, because the Prophet has not expressly mentioned the name of Israel, though it is sufficiently known that <hi type="italic">Ephraim</hi> includes the ten tribes.<div eID="gen44899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44900" type="x-p"/>As to the words, since the particle <foreign xml:lang="he">הוי</foreign> (<hi type="italic">hōī</hi>) very frequently denotes “wishing evil on a person,” I was unwilling to depart from the ordinary opinion of commentators, more especially because the Prophet openly threatens in this passage; yet if the translation, <hi type="italic">Alas the</hi> <hi type="italic">crown!</hi> be preferred, I have no objection.<div eID="gen44900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44901" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For the excellence of its glory shall be a fading flower</hi> <note n="210"> <div sID="gen44902" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44902" type="x-p"/> </note> The copulative <foreign xml:lang="he">ו</foreign> (<hi type="italic">vau</hi>) signifies <hi type="italic">for</hi> or <hi type="italic">because</hi>. He compares the “glory” and “excellence” of Israel to “a fading flower,” as will afterwards be stated. In general, he pronounces a curse on the wealth of the Israelites; for by the word “Crown” he means nothing else than the wicked confidence with which they were puffed up, and which proceeded from the excess of their riches. These vices are almost always joined together, because abundance and fullness produce cruelty and pride; for we are elated by prosperity, and do not know how to use it with moderation. They inhabited a rich and fertile country, and on this account Amos (<reference osisRef="Bible:Amos.4.1">Amos 4:1</reference>) calls them “fat cows,” which feed on the mountain of Samaria. Thus, being puffed up by their wealth, they despised both God and men. The Prophet calls them “drunkards,” because, being intoxicated by prosperity, they dreaded no adversity, and thought that they were beyond the reach of all danger, and that they were not even subject to God himself.<div eID="gen44901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44903" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">A fading flower.</hi> He alludes, I doubt not, to the crowns or chaplets <note n="211"> <div sID="gen44904" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44904" type="x-p"/> </note> which were used at banquets, and which are still used in many places in the present day. The Israelites indulged in gluttony and drunkenness, and the fertility of the soil undoubtedly gave occasion to their intemperance. By calling it “a fading flower” he follows out his comparison, elegantly alluding to flowers which suddenly wither.<div eID="gen44903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44905" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Which is on the head of the valley of fatness.</hi> <note n="212"> <div sID="gen44906" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen44906" type="x-p"/> </note> He says that that glory is “on the head of the valley of fatness,” because they saw under their feet their pastures, the fertility of which still more inflamed their pride. <foreign xml:lang="he">שמנים</foreign> (<hi type="italic">shĕmānīm</hi>) is translated by some “of ointments;” but that is inapplicable, for it denotes abundance and fullness, which led them to neglect godliness and to despise God. By the word “head” or “top,” he alludes to the position of the country, because the Israelites chiefly inhabited rich valleys. He places on it a crown, which surrounds the whole kingdom; because it was flourishing and abounded in every kind of wealth. This denotes riches, from which arose sluggishness, presumption, rashness, intemperance, and cruelty. This doctrine relates to us also; for the example of these men reminds us that we ought to use prosperity with moderation, otherwise we shall be very unhappy, for the Lord will curse all our riches and abundance.<div eID="gen44905" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.28.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen44897" osisID="Isa.28.1" type="section"/>
entries.6bbf4887e9fa28cf7e1ffe05fefa4d811b891132: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.28.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.28.2" sID="gen44907" type="section"/> <div sID="gen44908" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> <hi type="italic">Behold, the Lord hath a mighty and strong one.</hi> This may refer to the Assyrians, as if he had said, that they will be ready at God’s command to fight under his authority, as soon as they shall be called.
